en: Sutta Nipāta 2.12 Nigrodhakappa (Vaṅgīsa) Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Now at that time, the elder named Nigrodhakappa, the preceptor of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, had recently attained final nibbāna at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Then, while the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Has my preceptor attained final Nibbāna, or has he not yet attained final Nibbāna?
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Vaṅgīsa said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘Has my preceptor attained final Nibbāna, or has he not yet attained final Nibbāna?’”
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed him in verse:
“I ask the Teacher of peerless wisdom,
who cuts through doubt even in this very life.”
At Aggāḷava, a bhikkhu passed away—
one well-known, renowned, and with a mind fully extinguished.
"Nigrodhakappa" was his name.
"O Blessed One, this was done by that brahmin;
paying homage to it, he lived seeking liberation,
ardent in effort and firm in his vision of the Dhamma."
O All-Seeing One, we Śākyas, all of us, also desire to know that disciple;
our ears are poised for hearing.
You are our teacher; you are unsurpassed.
Cut through our doubt and speak this to us:
make known, O one of vast wisdom, that which has attained final Nibbāna.
Speak for us, O All-Seeing One,
like Sakka, the thousand-eyed lord of the gods;
whatever bonds there are here that lead to delusion—
Ignorance and the states of doubt—
these do not exist once one has reached the Tathāgata,
for this is the supreme eye among men.
For never indeed does a person dispel his defilements as the wind disperses clouds from the sky;
by darkness he is shrouded, the entire world.
Even radiant men would not outshine them;
the wise become makers of light, and that,
O hero, I consider to be exactly so.
We have come to you who possesses insight and knowledge;
reveal the Dhamma to us in the assemblies.
Quickly utter your lovely, most lovely voice!
Like a swan, lifting its voice, it coos slowly;
with a well-modulated, nasal tone,
we all hear it as it issues forth straightly.
Having utterly abandoned birth and death,
having restrained myself, I shall teach the Dhamma to the pure one;
for ordinary people do not act according to their own will.
This is the summary of the Tathāgatas;
this exposition of yours is perfect,
having been grasped by one of upright wisdom.
This is my final salutation with palms joined in reverence;
do not delude me, O you of peerless wisdom who knows the mind.
Having understood the noble Dhamma, both high and low, [I take refuge].
Do not delude me, O hero of the mind who knows;
like water for one scorched by heat in the summer heat,
I long for your words— rain down what has been heard.
Was the holy life lived by Kappāyana for its true purpose not in vain? Has he attained Nibbāna,
or does he still have a residue remaining?
“Hear from us how he became liberated.
“He cut off craving here for name-and-form,” said the Blessed One.
“The stream of Kaṇha, which had lain dormant for a long time,
has been crossed; he has transcended birth and death without remainder,” so said the Blessed One, the best of the five.
“Having heard this, I have faith in your words, O best of seers;
indeed, my question was not in vain.”
The brahmin has not deceived me;
as he spoke, so he acted—
he was a disciple of the Buddha.
He has torn the net of Death,
that strong snare spread by the Deceiver.
The Blessed One has seen the beginning.
“Kappiya was one who clung to grasping;
Kappāyana has indeed transcended the realm of death, so difficult to cross.”
The Nigrodhakappa Sutta, the twelfth.
